summary: Defines host multihoming extensions to the Host Identity Protocol, reusing the pieces built for mobility, so a host with several addresses can be reached through any of them.

eli5.summary: A person with two phone numbers can be reached on either. This lets a computer with several network addresses stay reachable on all.

questions: how does hip use multiple ip addresses
what is a preferred locator in hip
subtitle: How a Host Identity Protocol host with several IP addresses tells its peer and stays reachable on any of them.

tldr.problem: A host can have several IP addresses at once, on one or more interfaces. HIP ties security to host identities, not addresses, so it needs a way to tell a peer about all the addresses where the host can be reached.
tldr.mechanism: The host reuses the LOCATOR_SET parameter from the HIP mobility specification, sent in R1, I2, R2 or UPDATE packets, optionally with ESP_INFO to create new security associations, and marks one locator as preferred.
tldr.outcome: A host can use extra addresses for fault tolerance or load balancing. Policy such as which locator to choose is left open, and new addresses must be verified before use.

sections.title: Scope and Setting
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) from RFC 7401 decouples the transport layer from the internetworking layer by using public and private key pairs, not IP addresses, as host identities. Transport sockets and ESP security associations (SAs) bind to those identities, and IP addresses are only used for packet forwarding.

That makes new solutions for mobility and host multihoming possible. Basic mobility is defined in RFC 8046, which also specifies the LOCATOR_SET parameter that carries addresses between peers. Multihoming is somewhat the dual case: a host has more than one point of attachment at the same time.

This document covers messaging and procedure for some basic host multihoming scenarios. It largely assumes the ESP transport format of RFC 7402. Site multihoming and the Shim6 protocol of RFC 5533 are mentioned, but this RFC adds no site multihoming extensions. Transport congestion control, path MTU selection and QoS responses are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Normally a computer is known by its address. HIP instead gives it a name that never changes, and addresses are just where to deliver mail. This RFC is about what to do when the computer has several delivery addresses.

sections.title: Multihoming Model and Background
sections.content:
In mobility, a host has locators one after another. In multihoming it has multiple locators simultaneously. Using the LOCATOR_SET parameter, a host announces additional locators, and it may designate one as preferred, meaning the peer should send packets there before trying another. A host may also leave the preferred bit unset on all addresses and let the peer choose.

In the base specification, the HIP base exchange sets up one SA in each direction, so there is one source address, one destination address, one inbound SA and one outbound SA. In HIP, host IDs rather than IP addresses are conceptually the selectors in the security policy database. Inbound, the ESP SPI alone may be used to find the SA.

An address has a state: UNVERIFIED, ACTIVE, VERIFIED or DEPRECATED. Newly learned peer addresses must be verified before being put into active service, and addresses the peer removes are deprecated. A Locator Type of 1 binds an address to an ESP SPI.

The RFC does not define all policy. Which locator to choose, simultaneous mobility and multihoming, source address selection beyond RFC 6724, and transport implications are left out.
sections.eli5: Moving is like changing houses one at a time. Multihoming is like living in two houses at once. A computer lists its houses, says which is favorite, and the friend checks each address works before sending important mail there.

sections.title: Usage Scenarios
sections.content:
Fault tolerance. A host with more than one interface or address sends a LOCATOR_SET in an R1, I2 or R2 packet, or later in an UPDATE. By default the address used in the base exchange is its preferred locator until indicated otherwise. For fault tolerance a single SA with several addresses is likely enough, and the alternatives are used only when failure of the current address is detected. Failure detection techniques are outside the scope.

Load balancing. The host sends a LOCATOR_SET with an ESP_INFO whose OLD SPI is zero and whose NEW SPI is the new inbound SPI, asking for a new SA. A Type 1 locator ties the new address to the new SPI, and a second Type 1 locator keeps the original address and SPI. Each LOCATOR_SET MUST list all locators in use on the connection. The RFC suggests a separate SA pair for each path being balanced, to avoid anti-replay window problems.

Both hosts multihomed. If each host requests new SAs for new addresses, the result can be a full mesh of SAs. With n addresses on one host and m on the other, as many as n * m SAs in each direction are possible, at the cost of signaling and state in the SPD and SAD.

Mobility together with multihoming. A host can be both, for example with interfaces on different access technologies where one keeps its address while another changes. LOCATOR_SET plus ESP_INFO is expected to handle most such cases, but complicated ones have not been studied.

Across addressing realms. The mechanisms can migrate an association between IPv4 and IPv6. If the two hosts end up only using locators in different realms, some separate interworking mechanism is needed.
sections.eli5: If one road is blocked, use the other (fault tolerance). If you have two roads and a lot to carry, send trucks on both (load balancing). Each road can get its own lockbox key so the deliveries do not get mixed up.

sections.title: Packets That Carry Locators
sections.content:
A Responder MAY include a LOCATOR_SET in R1, protected by the R1 signature. If it carries a new preferred locator, the Initiator SHOULD set it ACTIVE without verifying first and MUST send the I2 to that locator. Non-preferred locators still need verification after the base exchange. Because I1 and I2 may then come from different source addresses, a Responder that pre-creates R1 packets indexed by Initiator address must make its puzzle indexing flexible enough.

An Initiator MAY put one or more LOCATOR_SET parameters in I2, protected by the I2 signature. The Responder still MUST send R2 to the I2 source address. R2 can also carry a LOCATOR_SET, covered by HIP_MAC_2 and HIP_SIGNATURE, which suits a host that does not want to reveal more locators until I2 is processed.

In an UPDATE, the receiver answers with an UPDATE acknowledgment. In R1, I2 or R2, the base exchange retransmission mechanism confirms delivery. A LOCATOR_SET in R1 must use Type 0 locators since no SAs exist yet.
sections.eli5: A computer can mention its extra addresses while first saying hello, or later in a follow-up note. Mentioning them in the hello is useful when it wants friends to know its other addresses right from the start.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
When sending, the choice of when to send a LOCATOR_SET and which addresses to include is local policy. Broadcast and multicast addresses MUST NOT be announced. Link-local addresses MUST NOT be announced unless the peer is known to be on the same link. Locators for tunnel or other virtual interfaces MAY be announced, but implementations SHOULD avoid making them preferred when a more direct path exists.

A host SHOULD process ESP_INFO before LOCATOR_SET. The OLD SPI and NEW SPI values select one of four cases:

  • OLD equals NEW and exists: gratuitous, provided for middleboxes, no rekeying.
  • OLD exists and NEW is a different non-zero value: the SA is rekeyed.
  • OLD is zero and NEW is non-zero: a new SA is requested.
  • OLD exists and NEW is zero: the SA is deprecated, and locators bound only to it become DEPRECATED.

If none apply, a protocol error has occurred. Each Type 1 address is added or refreshed as UNVERIFIED, and addresses on that SPI that were not listed become DEPRECATED. Type 0 addresses become UNVERIFIED if previously unknown or deprecated, and the host may associate them with one or more SAs.

To change the preferred locator, an ACTIVE one is switched to at once. An UNVERIFIED one is verified first, and meanwhile the host SHOULD use a different ACTIVE locator, or MAY use the new one as far as Credit-Based Authorization permits. If the peer states no preference, the host picks an ACTIVE address randomly or by policy. If the target is DEPRECATED and a non-deprecated address exists, it chooses that one. An unsupported Locator Type on a preferred locator SHOULD trigger a NOTIFY error of type LOCATOR_TYPE_UNSUPPORTED.
sections.eli5: Each locator is like a house on a list. New houses are marked unchecked until proven reachable, houses taken off the list are marked old, and the computer only switches its favorite house when it is sure the new one works.

sections.title: Security Associations and Anti-Replay
sections.content:
A host may set up any number of SAs with a peer, mainly to group addresses that share fate or to balance load. In HIP the inbound IP address is not used to look up the SA. Different addresses usually mean different paths and latencies, so packets can be reordered and fall outside the ESP anti-replay window.

To prevent that, HIP lets an inbound SPI have an affinity for certain inbound addresses, communicated to the peer. Each physical interface SHOULD have a separate SA, unless the anti-replay window is extended or disabled. A host SHOULD consistently send from the same source interface and address for a given destination address and SPI. It may be useful to change the SPI or reset the anti-replay window when the peer readdresses.
sections.eli5: Each package carries a number so a copy cannot sneak in twice. If packages take roads of different speed, they can arrive out of order and look suspicious, so each road gets its own numbering.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most security considerations of RFC 8046 carry over, because the strong authentication used for mobility also protects multihoming. The RFC compares against the threats in RFC 4218. Locators are listed in HIP packets signed with the identifier key, which addresses the binding of locators to an identifier. Classic and premeditated redirection are prevented by strong authentication, third-party DoS by address verification, and replay by ESP replay protection.

A malicious peer could send too many candidate locators or many UPDATEs, so implementations should consider limiting accepted locators and rate limiting UPDATEs. Exposing addresses may be a privacy concern for hosts hiding behind a VPN, so implementations SHOULD let the administrator block exposure of selected addresses or ranges. Implementors are also warned about traffic leaking outside the ESP-protected envelope when several addresses are used.
sections.eli5: Every address announcement is signed, so nobody can pretend to be you and steal your mail. The computer also checks that an address really works, and should not accept a flood of addresses.

messages.note: Asks for a new SA and announces the new address.

messages.note: New outbound SA, plus address verification.

messages.label: I2
messages.note: Sent to the newly indicated preferred address.

messages.label: R2
messages.note: Processed normally; non-preferred locators are verified later.

items.label: No rekeying
items.desc: Both are an existing SPI; the ESP_INFO is gratuitous, for middleboxes.

items.label: Rekeying
items.desc: OLD is an existing SPI and NEW is a different non-zero value.

items.label: New SA
items.desc: The peer is requesting a new SA with a non-zero NEW SPI.

items.label: Deprecating the SA
items.desc: Locators bound only to that SPI become DEPRECATED.
